name: Laser lipolysis (SmartLipo)
lead: Laser lipolysis, also called laser-assisted liposuction or by the SmartLipo brand, passes a thin laser fiber through a small incision under the skin to disrupt fat cells, sometimes followed by suction removal.[1][7][17] It is used on small, stubborn areas such as the neck and jawline, arms, abdomen and flanks, with the aim of a slimmer contour and, as proponents claim, tighter skin over the treated area.[1][7][17] For appearance, the jawline and under-chin area is a common target: removing a small fat pocket there sharpens the line between jaw and neck.

Reviews describe the laser as an adjunct to liposuction that induces lipolysis and hemostasis and is proposed to stimulate new collagen; early reports described a less traumatic technique than conventional liposuction with less bleeding and skin retraction.[1][5][17] Subsequent work includes a 30-subject Nd:YAG study, histologic and thermal studies, and a retrospective analysis of 534 procedures with a diode laser.[2][3][4][8] Wikipedia says liposuction became the most common US cosmetic procedure in 2015 and lists laser-assisted liposuction among its main variants.[11]

The word choice matters: a 2009 review separates suction-assisted liposuction, laser lipolysis (melting fat without suction) and laser-assisted liposuction (laser followed by suction).[18] Clinics market the technique as SmartLipo, and Wikipedia describes it as using laser energy to firm skin and support collagen rather than relying on suction alone.[11]

angle.text: People choose laser lipolysis to reduce small fat pockets, such as under the chin or around the jawline, with the goal of a leaner outline. Heating the tissue is also claimed to tighten skin, which was a main selling point from the first reports.

infobox: Chin and jawline, neck, arms, abdomen, flanks[1][7]

paras: A thin laser fiber is introduced through a small incision into subcutaneous fat. The laser interacts with fat tissue, and the loosened fat may then be suctioned.[1] Authors describe a less traumatic technique than conventional liposuction, and some reviews report that it offers fewer side effects than liposuction performed under general anaesthesia, while noting that an objective comparison with tumescent liposuction is missing from the literature.[1][17]

Laser-assisted liposuction is one entry in a long line of liposuction variants Wikipedia lists: suction-assisted, tumescent, power-assisted, water-jet, ultrasound-assisted and radiofrequency-assisted.[11] A German review of physical lipolysis methods places laser lipolysis alongside focused-ultrasound, cryolipolysis, radiofrequency and HIFU treatments for diet- and exercise-resistant fat deposits.[23]

People choose laser lipolysis to reduce small fat pockets, such as under the chin or around the jawline, with the goal of a leaner outline; a 2016 paper describes a combination approach to neck rejuvenation that includes laser lipolysis.[7] The skin-tightening claim has been central since the first reports, which described skin retraction in flaccid areas.[1]

Wikipedia also lists non-cosmetic uses of laser-assisted liposuction, including reducing 'cankles' (a 2014 prospective study of 30 patients) and debulking in lipedema (a 2014 report in elderly patients combining it with a thigh lift and partial abdominoplasty).[11] A 2020 review covers laser-assisted techniques used during facelift surgery.[25]

Wikipedia traces modern liposuction to the French surgeon Charles Dujarier's 1926 case, then to Arpad and Giorgio Fischer in Rome in the mid-1970s, whose 1977 review of 245 cases reported a 4.9 percent seroma rate, then Yves-Gerard Illouz's extension to the whole body and Jeffrey Klein's tumescent anaesthesia method in the 1980s.[11] Laser lipolysis followed in the early 2000s: a 2002 article described laser lipolysis for flaccid areas, a 2005 study examined the pulsed Nd:YAG laser histologically, and a 2006 randomised, double-blind trial compared laser-assisted with suction-assisted lipoplasty.[1][4][19] A 2008 review described laser-assisted liposuction as the next step in body contouring, aiming to facilitate liposuction, tighten tissue and reduce downtime.[21]

A 2009 clinics-in-plastic-surgery report describes the Nd:YAG laser as addressing the main limitation of traditional lipoplasty, large-volume blood loss, and compares histologic and morphometric effects with the traditional method.[5] In 2015, liposuction surpassed breast augmentation as the most common US cosmetic procedure.[11] The same year the FDA approved deoxycholic acid (Kybella), an injectable for fat under the chin, on 29 April 2015, which became a non-surgical alternative for the same area.[24]

Histologic work on a pulsed Nd:YAG device (SmartLipo) examined its effects on excised human fat tissue.[4] Other studies compared wavelengths of 1064, 1320 and 2100 nm ex vivo,[9] and examined tissue temperature rise during 1064/1320 nm treatment.[3] A mathematical modeling paper described laser lipolysis heat effects,[6] and a study compared a 1,444 nm laser with a 1,064 nm laser, reporting a superior lipolytic effect for the former.[10] The 2012 review notes that lipolysis occurs in a dose-response manner and that standardisation of laser energy settings is lacking.[17] A 2009 clinical study examined serum lipid changes following laser lipolysis.[22]

An early report described skin retraction in flaccid areas.[1] A 2006 study of 30 subjects with small fat areas used a 1,064 nm Nd:YAG laser, with MRI in some participants at baseline and 3 months.[2] A 2009 retrospective analysis of 534 procedures with a 980 nm diode laser has been published,[8] a 2009 study examined laser lipolysis of the arm with and without suction,[20] and a 2016 paper described a combination approach to neck rejuvenation including laser lipolysis.[7]

The 2012 review of 19 manuscripts identified one double-blind randomised trial comparing laser liposuction with tumescent liposuction and concluded that laser-assisted lipolysis is safe and efficacious and may have advantages over conventional liposuction, while noting limited comparisons between laser systems and wavelengths.[17]

sections.h: Who it is for and what to expect
paras: Wikipedia's liposuction article says cosmetic liposuction is believed to work best for people of normal weight with good skin elasticity and that it is a body-contouring procedure rather than a weight-loss treatment; it also reports that fat can return and redistribute, often to the abdomen, in the months after surgery.[11]

Liposuction is commonly performed with the tumescent technique, in which a large volume of dilute lidocaine and epinephrine is infiltrated into the fat so the tissue is firm and bleeding is limited before suction; small-volume cases under about 1,000 cc may be done awake, while large-volume cases require anaesthesia and sometimes a hospital stay.[11] The article says swelling can persist for weeks or months and that a 2015 study found complication risk rose when volume removed exceeded about 100 ml per unit of BMI.[11]

Liposuction in general has reported complications including infection, bleeding, numbness, seroma and contour irregularities; Wikipedia cites a 2015 study of 4,534 patients with complications in 1.5 percent, and serious events such as deep vein thrombosis, organ perforation and fat embolism, with deaths reported at roughly one per ten thousand cases as of 2011.[11] Thermal studies of laser lipolysis examine how much tissue heating occurs at different wavelengths and techniques.[3] Wikipedia notes that cosmetic benefits of liposuction are generally short-term in terms of body fat, which tends to return over months.[11]

Published human work is largely small prospective studies and retrospective series, plus one randomised comparison with suction-assisted lipoplasty.[1][2][8][19] Several small trials of related devices are registered: a 1440 nm laser for the mandible and submandibular area (n=12, completed),[13] an LED device for non-invasive lipolysis (n=10, terminated),[12] a 1060 nm diode laser with other energy for non-invasive fat reduction (n=39, completed),[15] laser therapy with aerobic exercise (n=36, terminated),[14] and a 1064 nm diode laser/RF study (withdrawn).[16] Results are not given in the available records.

lore.intro: Laser lipolysis is discussed by people seeking a sharper jawline or a leaner contour mainly as a lower-downtime alternative to conventional liposuction, with clinics marketing the SmartLipo name and skin tightening.[11][17]

claims.claim: The laser melts fat and tightens skin, giving a better result than suction alone.
claims.believers: Clinics and early reports describe skin retraction and collagen stimulation as the advantage of laser assistance.[1][11]
claims.experts: A 2012 review concluded laser-assisted lipolysis is safe and efficacious and may have advantages over conventional liposuction, while noting limited comparisons.[17]

claims.claim: Laser lipolysis has less downtime and bleeding than conventional liposuction.
claims.believers: Authors describe it as a less traumatic technique with reduced bleeding.[1][5]
claims.experts: The review notes an objective comparison with tumescent liposuction is missing from the literature.[17]

claims.claim: It is a good way to define the jawline and neck.
claims.believers: Neck rejuvenation approaches include laser lipolysis for small submental fat pockets.[7]
claims.experts: Published neck work is a combination-approach experience paper plus a small registered 1440 nm mandible trial.[7][13]

claims.believers: Treated fat cells are removed or destroyed, so the area stays slimmer.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that fat can return and redistribute in the months after liposuction, often to the abdomen.[11]

claims.claim: Higher-wavelength or newer lasers (1444 nm) work better.
claims.believers: Manufacturers promote newer wavelengths for stronger fat disruption.[10]
claims.experts: A study reported a superior lipolytic effect for 1,444 nm versus 1,064 nm, while the 2012 review notes limited comparisons between wavelengths and a lack of standard energy settings.[10][17]

claims.claim: Laser lipolysis is safer than liposuction.
claims.believers: Several authors claim fewer side effects than traditional liposuction under general anaesthesia.[17]
claims.experts: General liposuction complication data (1.5 percent in a 4,534-patient study) are cited, and thermal studies examine heating of tissue.[3][11]

card.summary: Laser-assisted fat removal that heats fat through a small cannula, with early studies reporting fat reduction and some skin tightening.
card.note: A minimally invasive surgical procedure; published work is mostly small series and tissue studies.

quick.overview:
Laser lipolysis, best known by the SmartLipo brand, is a minimally invasive procedure in which a laser fiber is passed through a small incision to liquefy or heat fat, often followed by suction. It is discussed in looksmaxxing spaces for the jawline and neck.

The early literature, much of it practitioner-written, reports fat reduction and skin tightening. Most published studies are small, histology or modeling studies, or retrospective series.
quick.mechanism: Laser energy at wavelengths such as 1064, 1320 or 1444 nm is absorbed by fat tissue, disrupting fat cells and heating the surrounding tissue. Authors claim the heating also stimulates collagen and skin contraction.
quick.risks: It is a surgical procedure with risks shared with liposuction, such as bleeding, infection, numbness and contour irregularities. Heating of tissue is a specific consideration, and thermal studies have examined temperature rise in treated tissue.
